summary: This memo is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1300 through RFC 1399, written as a status report on them. It marks which ones are on the standards track and points readers to the current official protocol standards list. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a table of contents for one hundred papers in the Internet series, with a short note about each one so you can find what you are looking for.

questions: what rfcs are in the standards track
subtitle: An index of 100 RFCs documenting the Internet standards process and protocols

tldr.problem: Finding relevant RFCs among thousands of documents is difficult without guidance on what each one covers.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists and briefly describes all 100 RFCs from 1300 to 1399, marking which ones define standards and grouping them by purpose.
tldr.outcome: Readers can quickly scan the catalog to find RFCs relevant to their work, and see which ones are on the standards track.

today: RFC 1399 is an informational document that served its purpose as a snapshot at the time. Later RFC summary documents cover more recent RFCs. Today, the RFC Index and online searchable databases serve the same purpose more effectively.

sections.title: What This Memo Is
sections.content: This memo is a catalog of the 100 RFCs numbered 1300 through 1399, published from February 1992 to January 1997. It provides a short description of each RFC and marks which ones define Internet standards as opposed to experimental or informational documents. The memo was written because the RFC series had grown large enough that finding relevant documents became difficult without such a guide.
sections.eli5: This is a table of contents for one hundred internet papers. Each entry tells you the number, title, and what the paper is about.

sections.title: What the 1300s RFCs Cover
sections.content: The RFCs from 1300 to 1399 span a wide range of topics. They include new protocols and extensions (like RIP Version 2 and TCP extensions for high performance), standards for network management (SNMP security, MIB definitions for various devices), mail and messaging systems (MIME format, message handling), domain naming and registration (DNS records, domain administration), and administrative documents about the standards process itself. Some RFCs are April 1st humor; one is a poem. Others are critical infrastructure documents describing how the Internet Registration Service transitioned between organizations.
sections.eli5: These papers describe routing protocols, network management systems, email formats, how to register domains, security improvements, and the tools the Internet community uses to stay organized.

sections.title: Standards Track Documents
sections.content: Many of the RFCs in this range are marked [STANDARDS-TRACK] in the memo. These are RFCs that have been processed through the Internet standardization process and represent protocols or practices that have been formally approved or are on the path to approval. The standards track includes protocols from internet layers (like IP encapsulation on FDDI networks), routing protocols (BGP, OSPF), mail extensions (MIME), and network management tools. Not all RFCs are standards-track; some are purely informational documents, experimental protocols, or administrative guidance.
sections.eli5: Some papers describe things the Internet officially agrees everyone should use. Others are just information or experiments that might not become standards.

sections.title: Key Areas Covered
sections.content: The 1300s RFCs document several major areas of Internet development. Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) and its variants make up a significant portion, with RFCs defining how PPP works and how different network protocols run over it. Network management is heavily represented through SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) security documents and MIB (Management Information Base) definitions for managing everything from Ethernet interfaces to character devices. The series also includes important work on routing (RIP version 2, OSPF applicability, BGP interactions), address space management as the Internet grew, encryption and digest algorithms (MD2, MD4, MD5), and the transition of Internet registration services to the InterNIC.
sections.eli5: These papers cover how computers talk to each other over phone lines, how to monitor and manage networks, how the Internet finds routes to send packets, and the growing pains of assigning addresses as the Internet expanded.
